Anaerobic digestion of corn straw pretreated by ultrasonic combined with 
aerobic hydrolysis 
Xiaodong Chu a,b, Qiushuang Cheng a, Yonghua Xu c, Lina Luo a, Ming Wang a, Guoxiang Zheng a, 
Hongqiong Zhang a, Weiming Yi d, Xiaofeng Liu e, Yongming Sun f, Yong Sun a,* 
a College of engineering Northeast Agriculture University, Harbin 15000, PR China 
b Key Laboratory of Renewable Energy, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Guangzhou 510640, PR China 
c College of electrical and information Northeast Agriculture University, Harbin 15000, PR China 
d College of Agricultural Engineering and Food Science, Shandong University of Technology, Zibo, Shandong 255000, PR China 
e Key Laboratory of Environmental and Applied Microbiology, Environmental Microbiology Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu Institute of Biology, Chinese 
Academy of Sciences, Chengdu 610041, PR China 
f Guangzhou Institute of Energy Conversion, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Guangzhou 510640, PR China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
• An effective way was studied for corn straw fermentation experiment. 
• The lag phase of fermentation can accelerate after ultrasonic pretreatment. 
• The performance of AD and the yield of methane can improve by ultrasonic pretreatment. 
• The highest cumulative methane production was 198.56 mL/g VS, 46.73% higher than untreated group.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Corn straw 
Ultrasonic 
Aerobic hydrolysis 
Anaerobic digestion 
Methane production 
A B S T R A C T   
Corn straw (CS) was pretreated by ultrasonic combined aerobic with biogas slurry as medium for anaerobic 
digestion (AD), that strengthened the degradation efficiency CS, varied in the composition of digestion slurry, 
thereby the methane production was increased. Central combinatorial design (CCD) test was used to treat CS at 
ultrasonic power (200, 400, and 600 W), time (10, 20, and 30 min) and AD for 25 days, at 37 ± 1℃. According to 
data showed that the pH and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) affected methane production directly. With an ultrasonic 
power 309 W, time 26 min, it reached the maximum content of VFAs with 16.24 g/L, the cumulative methane 
production achieved the highest with 198.56 mL/g VS, which was 46.73% higher than unpretreated raw material 
as CK. Ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pretreatment can obtain higher VFAs and methane production content in a 
short period of time that is great significance to biogas engineering.   
1. Introduction 
Since 2014, China has made great efforts to solve the adverse impact 
of corn straw (CS), and proposed that taking advantage of CS for AD to 
produce methane can not only solve the problem of CS, but also provide 
energy (Chen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019). The use of AD to trans­
form biomass raw materials into biomass energy has been the most 
widely resource utilization way in China, meanwhile, the products of 
reaction are also widely used to achieve zero pollution (Lorena, et al., 
2018; Sun et al., 2020). However, due to the complex structure of cell 
walls of CS, anaerobic microorganisms cannot directly break through 
the lignocellulosic construction to utilize, so it is vital to apply pre­
treatment ways to improve the efficiency of AD (Liu et al., 2017). Up to 
now, the common pretreatment methods mainly include physical, 
chemical, biological, ultrasonic pretreatment, steam explosion and 
liquid hot water pretreatment (Zhong et al., 2018; Syaftika and Matsu­
mura, 2018; Zou et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017). 
For instance, Wang et al. (2019) found that the pretreatment of CS 
with production wastewater from furfural plant could increased the 
content of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) in the substrate and effectively

increased cumulative methane production. Kang et al. (2018) reported 
that hemicellulose and lignin were removed by alkali pretreated and the 
yield of methane production increased by 21%. Some researcher re­
ported that used efficient white rot fungus strains to treat CS to improve 
the porosity and crystallinity of lignocellulose in AD process (Rouches 
et al. 2017; Zhao et al., 2020; Chu et al. 2020). Above mentioned acid, 
alkali and biological pretreated methods, usually purported expensive 
cost prior to AD. Therefore, it is urgent to find an efficient and pollution- 
free method to preprocess CS before AD. Ultrasonic pretreatment was 
proposed the most popular technologies to accelerate the biochemical 
process of microorganisms, recently (Yang and Fang, 2014; Zheng et al., 
2014), with advantages of easy operation and good effect in producing 
gas. The ultrasonic pretreated method has been mature and applied in 
many large and medium-sized methane projects gradually (Batghare 
et al., 2018). 
A large number of studies showed that ultrasonic technology could 
rupture and deform fiber cells, or break the hydrogen bonds between 
fiber molecules, and increase the inner surface area. (Hassan, et al., 
2018; Subhedar and Gogate, 2014). Fakayode et al. (2020) used ultra­
sonic and deep eutectic solvent pretreatment to continuously removed 
43.56% of lignin from watermelon, at ultrasonic power of 180 W. Bus­
semaker et al. (2013) found that the low-frequency ultrasound could 
result in the deploy-merization of lignin matrix through the cleavage of 
α-o-4 and β-o-4 bonds, and free radicals also caused the rupture of ligno- 
carbohydrate bond, and releasing hemicellulose. The United States, 
United Kingdom, Australia and other countries have begun to use ul­
trasonic technology to treat waste activated sludge. Chen et al. (2014) 
investigated that it could effectively reduce the volatile solid (VS) or­
ganics and increase biogas production by more than 40% on average. 
Therefore, it is very desirable that use the ultrasonic method to promote 
the disintegration of CS (Srisowmeya et al., 2020). The introduction of 
aerobic hydrolysis in the process of AD and the establishment of a 
unique micro-oxygen environment has a positive impact on microbial 
metabolism (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018; Nguyen et al., 2019). In addi­
tion, the addition of low-oxygen micro-aerobic conditions in the 
anaerobic digester can significantly increase the degradation rate of 
lignocellulose and the methane production in the anaerobic process (Fu 
et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2018). 
The main purposes of this research are: (1) to inquire into the 
changes of pretreatment slurry at synergistic effect of ultrasonic and 
oxygen hydrolysis; (2) to analyze lignocellulosic degradation rate, 
reducing sugar content, VFAs, pH and cumulative methane production 
of CS in AD; and (3) to use the response surface optimization analysis to 
find the optimum proposal for improving VFAs. This research provides 
an economical and practical way for the pretreatment of complex raw 
materials during the operation of biogas projects. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Digestion substrate 
After natural air drying, the CS was crushed into 0.5–1 cm pieces and 
stored for use later. Inoculum and CS were cultivated in the laboratory of 
Northeast Agricultural University in Harbin, China. The characteristics 
of the inoculum and CS are presented in Table 1. All other chemicals and 
solvents are analytical grade. 
2.2. Experiment design 
Accurately weigh 10 g of raw material and CS by ultrasonic treated 
and put them in 100 mesh cotton filter bags, seal and press into the 
biogas slurry, keep the water bath at 37 ◦C for 0.5 h, 1.0 h, 2 h, 4 h, 6 h, 8 
h, 12 h and 16 h, thereby take it out, rinse off the impurities with water, 
drain for 5 min until no more dripping, measure moisture content. 
The test is divided into two parts: ultrasonic combined aerobic hy­
drolysis pretreatment and AD. The ultrasonic pretreatment device used 
in this experiment was designed and developed by the Chemistry Lab­
oratory of Northeast Agricultural University. The ultrasonic control 
device, ultrasonic generator and acoustic chamber together form the 
entire ultrasonic pretreatment device. The ultrasonic control apparatus 
including the power, duration time and temperature. The ultrasonic 
generator consists of an immersion probe with a diameter of 1.5 cm and 
a length of 19 cm. They can emit ultrasonic waves in both horizontal (X- 
axis) and vertical (Z-axis) directions. The ultrasonic frequency of the 
device is 20 kHz, and the maximum power of the device is 900 W. 
Adjust the lug of the lifting platform so that the transmitting end of 
the ultrasonic probe is immersed in the solution of 10–30 mm of the 
liquid level (working volume: 200 mL). 40 g CS (moisture content 
11.58%) and 400 mL biogas slurry with TS of 5% were mixed in 1000 mL 
beaker, and placed them under the generator for ultrasonic combined 
aerobic hydrolysis pretreatment, for the different ultrasonic power and 
time to ger pretreatment slurry, at 25℃. The experiment was divided 
into two groups with 3 parallels, one was used for the detection of the 
slurry composition after ultrasonic pretreatment, and the other was all 
transferred to the subsequent AD. The experimental conditions of the 
two groups are exactly the same. They were carried out in a constant 
temperature water bath at 37 ◦C for 25 days, with regular shaking once a 
day to keep the materials uniform. 40 g unpretreated CS and 400 mL 
biogas slurry were used as substrate of CK, and adjust the substrate TS to 
5% for AD immediately. 
2.3. Central composite design 
CCD test was used to explore the response of power and time of the 
ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pretreatment to the VFAs index, and the 
second-order RSM was usually applied to fitting to optimize the argu­
ments of ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pretreatment conditions. Among 
them, power, time of two independent variables are respectively turned 
into coded A, B and divided into 5 levels: -λ, −1, 0, 1, λ. On the basis of 
previous study, in this study determined the range of independent var­
iables in the CCD test. The encoding values of the independent variables 
and the actual values of the preprocessing conditions are shown in 
Table 2. At the same time, a multiple linear regression model was 
selected to analyze the response of ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pre­
treatment to the content of VFAs as shown in Eq. (1):

2.4. Index measurement method 
The samples are measured with differential gravimetric method for 
TS, VS and pH (pHS-25). Under standard atmospheric pressure, deter­
mine the water absorption rate of CS. Elemental analyzer is used for the 
determination of carbon and nitrogen (EA 3000, LEEMAN). The ligno­
cellulose is measured using a Van Soest fiber analyzer (Ankom200i, 
Anko Borui Technology Beijing, China). The composition of biogas and 
VFAs are analyzed using different modules of gas chromatograph (GC- 
6890 N, Agilent Inc.).

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of pretreatment on the physical and chemical properties of CS 
3.1.1. Effect of pretreatment on water absorption rate of CS 
In this experiment, the C3:259 W-27 min, C6:600 W-20 min and 
C9:400 W-20 min groups were selected to determine the water absorp­
tion of CS and compared with CK. Fig. 1 (a) showed that the water ab­
sorption rate of CS increased with time before 6 h, and then remained 
unchanged after increasing to a certain value. The higher water ab­
sorption rate of CK, C3:259 W-27 min, C6:600 W-20 min and C9:400 W- 
20 min were 209.15%, 252.62%, 258.68% and 267.44%, respectively. 
The treatment groups showed better water absorption capacity, due to 
the increase in the pore density of CS of the cellulose skeleton at the 
conditions of ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis treatment, and the water 
molecules can get into the CS quickly (Dong and Chen, 2019; Velmur­
ugan and Muthukumar, 2012). In the mid-term, the water absorption 
strength of CS decreased, because of the water in the CS was saturated 
and the diffusion rate decreased. The water absorption rate of CS 
decreased after 12 h, because the increase of cell wall rupture led to the 
decrease of water retention performance of CS. In summary, a certain 
degree of ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pretreatment could expose more 
cellulose, expand the pore density of CS, and showed higher water 
absorption. 
3.1.2. Effect of pretreatment on lignocellulosic of CS 
The physical structure of CS treated by ultrasonic directly reflects the 
availability of this pretreatment method. Hence, it is very vital to 
quantitatively analyze and evaluate the degradation of lignocellulosic 
substances in CS (Guan et al., 2018). It can be seen from Table 4 that 
hemicellulose exhibited stronger degradability, with a degradation rate 
ranging from 28.29% to 38.51%. Secondly, the degradability of cellu­
lose was 15.58%-30.17%, and the degradability of lignin was the 
weakness, which was 3.52%–8.69%. It was possible that ultrasonic 
cavitation broken hydrogen bonds, glycoside bonds in hemicellulose 
and showed higher degradability, enhanced CS solubilization (Kim 
et al., 2018; Qi et al., 2021). Due to the intensity of cavitation bubble 
effect loosened lignocellulose structure, exposed a larger number of 
enzyme action sites, which was more conducive to the degradation of 
lignocellulose (Rehman et al., 2014). 
3.1.3. Scanning electron microscope analysis 
Observed the CS of C9:400 W-20 min and CK through a scanning 
electron microscope 2000 times, we found that the surface of the wood 
fiber of CK was relatively smooth. Because there was no obvious holes in 
the surface of the vertical wood fiber, it is difficult for the hydrolase to 
enter the CS. The results of C9:400 W-20 min showed obvious holes and 
many “fragments”, as same time, the cellulose was stripped, and a sense 
of layering appeared. Ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis treatment signifi­
cantly changed the structure of CS, and the surface of CS collapsed, 
indicating that the lignin removal effect was obvious. Compared with 
the ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pretreatment, the CS has no obvious 
changes in the macroscopic view. However, under the electron micro­
scope lens, the structure of the CS has changed significantly. Due to the 
effect of hydrolytic enzymes on the lignocellulose, and part of the 
hemicellulose and cellulose were degraded (Guan et al., 2018). 
3.2. Effect of ultrasonic - aerobic hydrolysis on digestion slurry 
3.2.1. Effect of ultrasonic - aerobic hydrolysis on reducing sugars 
The degree of ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis on the hydrolysis and 
utilization of lignocellulose in CS, ultimately affect the performance of 
subsequent AD to produce methane (Hu et al., 2017). Variations of 
reducing sugar yields in pretreatment slurry directly reflected the per­
formance of the hydrolysis stage under different ultrasonic-aerobic hy­
drolysis, was showed in Fig. 1(b). In all pretreated samples, the reducing 
sugar yields of pretreated C1:200 W-20 min, C2:541 W-13 min…C9:400 
W-20 min varied among 8.31–13.79 mg/mL, which the highest one was 
C3 at ultrasonic power of 259 W and 27 min; the lowest one was C6 at 
ultrasonic power of 600 W, time in 20 min. Under the action of 
ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis, polar molecules contained in the CS could 
rub against each other violently, made the biomass surface with 
increased affinity for enzyme attack (Hu et al., 2017). Hence, the hy­
drolase was easily to enter the binding site of hydrolase to catalyze, 
accelerated hydrolyzed cellulose and hemicellulose into educing sugars 
such as glucose and xylose, provided abundant digestive substrate and 
carbon source for AD (Zou et al., 2016; Qi et al., 2020). However, 
excessive ultrasonic power would accelerate the degradation of reducing 
sugars, and decrease of pH in the digestion environment, which was not 
conducive to the survival of microorganisms and hydrolysis activities, 
and impact to the stability of hydrolysis system. 
3.2.2. Effect of ultrasonic aerobic hydrolysis on VFAs and pH 
Since methanogens cannot directly decompose and utilize macro­
molecular organic matter, but use VFAs such as acetic acid to convert 
into methane gas. Consequently, VFAs has become a key intermediate in 
the process of converting organic matter to methane (Liu et al., 2019). 
Variations of VFAs during the pretreated groups were shown in Fig. 1(c). 
The results displayed that the highest VFAs reached 16.24 g/L in C9:400 
W-20 min; the lowest one was 8.45 g/L in C5:259 W-13 min. Ultrasonic 
pretreatment can make the carbohydrates are consumed and utilized by 
acid-producing bacteria into organic acids faster, thereby the VFAs 
increased in pretreated slurry (Lizama et al., 2017). As showed in Fig. 1 
(d), the pH value all maintain generally between- 5.89–7.32. Due to the 
accumulation of VFAs lead to the pH drop drastically, the higher VFAs is 
contrary the lower pH value. Among the all pretreatments, the compo­
nents of VFAs all showed the main VFAs in each treated groups were 
acetic acid, followed by butyric acid, propionic acid, and a very small 
amount of valeric acid. The VFAs can be used by acidogenic and ace­
togenic bacteria convert VFAs into acetate, H2, and CO2, which are used

3.3. Effect of ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis on methane production in AD 
The methane production of CS treated by ultrasonic-aerobic hydro­
lysis are shown in Table 5. The lowest and the highest treated groups are 
C1:200 W-20 min and C9:400 W-20 min, which are 154.32 mL/g VS and 
196.13 mL/g VS, respectively. Compared with CK group, it has increased 
by 14.04%-52.33%. The ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis make the mono­
saccharides, and oligosaccharides are more readily water-soluble, and 
decompose by microorganisms and fungi quickly, and increase the 
initial VFAs content in the digestion slurry, thereby improving the 
methanogenesis characteristics of CS in AD. Among them, the fitting 
coefficient R2 is greater than 0.98, indicating that the fitting effect is 
better (Yang et al., 2019). It can be seen that as the strength of aerobic 
hydrolysis increases, the lag time becomes shorter. The λ values of CK, 
C1:200 W-20 min, C2:541 W-13 min,…C9:400 W-20 min are: 1.37, 0.24, 
0.39, 0.36, 0.18, 0.46, 0.66, 0.23, 0.58 and 0.28. The λ values of treat­
ment groups were shorter than CK, significantly. 
This relatively shorter lag phase indicated that the activity of 
methanogens is high at moderate pH, adapt the substrate faster, shortens 
the lag time of AD, resulting in a higher methane yield (Mainardis et al., 
2019; Pellera and Gidarakos, 2016). Fig. 3 is a graph of cumulative 
methane production content, and Gompertz fitting was performed by 
origin 2017, and the fitting results are shown in the figure. The cumu­
lative methane content of each experimental group is different, the cu­
mulative methane production of the treated groups are higher than CK 
significant, and the difference between the groups was not significant. 
The above results showed that the pretreatment could effectively in­
crease the cumulative methane production content (Ya) of AD, which is 
similar to the fitting data conclusion (Ym), indicating the fitting effect 
better. The main reason is that the hydrolase has improved cellulose 
degradation ability in the digestion system, and increased the VFAs in 
the initial stage of digestion. The ability of hydrogen and methanogens 
to VFAs has also been improved, and better treatment effect.

than time, meanwhile, the effect of ultrasonic power on VFAs is signif­
icant (p < 0.05). For the effect of ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pre­
treatment, aggravate the damage to CS, improve the degradation of 
lignocellulose and increase VFAs effectively. The time of ultrasonic- 
aerobic hydrolysis treatment is shorter than that time of aerobic hy­
drolysis. The results indicated that the introduction of ultrasonic waves 
can not only reduce the intensity of aerobic hydrolysis, short the time, 
but also increase the VFAs. 
As shown in Fig. 2(a) and (b), within a certain range, VFAs will in­
crease with the increase of the ultrasonic power and time. When the 
pretreatment conditions are 309 W and 26 min, VFAs reached the 
maximum value and no longer increases.Fig. 3 
4. Conclusion 
The study suggested that ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pretreatment 
mainly changed the degradation lignocellulose rate and improved the 
methane production by increasing VFAs in slurry. Through RSM anal­
ysis, the effect of power on VFAs was obviously greater than that of time. 
The highest VFAs (16.24 g/L) was achieved by the pretreatment 309 W 
and 26 min, thereby methane production reached 198.56 mL/g VS, 
which was 46.73% higher than CK. Therefore, this study recommended 
ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis application for shortened the time and 
hydrolysis of CS effectively. Finally, using the potential to handle bulk 
amount of CS can be helpful in industrial applications.
